choices.why: Right: the run cannot say which reading the model took.

choices.text: The model knew the label was wrong
choices.why: The label was right.

prompt: Why is calibration checked over many answers and never one?

choices.text: A single answer cannot refute 0.85
choices.why: Right: a stated 0.85 is a claim about a rate, and a rate needs many answers.

choices.text: Single answers have no confidence field
choices.why: Every reply here carries one.

choices.text: `calibrate.py` refuses fewer than ten replies
choices.why: It does not; it would print a thin table.

choices.text: Confidence only means something above 0.9
choices.why: Every bin makes a claim that can be checked.

prompt: The 46 replies that stated 0.8: what share of them was right? Two decimal places.
On a reliability diagram, a bin's point sits below the diagonal. What does that say?
hint: Stated is along, accuracy is up.

choices.text: That bin said less than it achieved
choices.why: That would put the point above the line.

choices.text: The bin is too small to read
choices.why: Size is the `n` beside it, not where it sits.

choices.text: The answers in that bin did not parse
choices.why: Only parsed replies with a confidence are binned.

choices.text: Overconfident: it said more than it delivered
choices.why: Right: accuracy below the confidence it stated.

prompt: The replies stated at 0.9 were right 0.78 of the time, and those stated at 0.8 were right 0.72. What does that closeness say?

choices.text: The model is perfectly calibrated in both bins
choices.why: Both points are below the diagonal.

choices.text: The model is underconfident
choices.why: It said more than it delivered.

choices.text: The 0.9 group is too small to read anything into
choices.why: Twenty-three is the smaller, not a tiny, bin.

choices.text: It barely separates right from wrong
choices.why: Right: two groups almost equally right.

prompt: Forty-six replies of 70 stated 0.80 and were right 0.72 of the time. How much does that bin add to the ECE? Three decimal places.
The score that averages, over every reply, the squared difference between stated confidence and 1 or 0 is the ___ score.
hint: Named after the meteorologist who proposed it.

prompt: A model states 0.80 on every reply and is right 80% of the time. What do ECE and Brier say about it?
hint: ECE compares the number with the rate; Brier asks whether it separates right from wrong.

choices.text: Both say it is perfect
choices.why: Brier charges it 0.16 for separating nothing.

choices.text: Both say it is badly calibrated
choices.why: Its number matches its rate exactly.

choices.text: ECE is zero; Brier still charges it
choices.why: Right: calibrated, and useless for telling which reply to trust.

choices.text: ECE needs more than one bin
choices.why: One bin is enough; its gap is zero.

prompt: Stating 0.74 on every reply would have scored a Brier of 0.19. The model's own numbers scored 0.212. What does that say?

choices.text: Brier cannot compare a constant
choices.why: It compares any confidence.

choices.text: The numbers carry less than the base rate
choices.why: Right: a constant beat them.

choices.text: The model is perfectly calibrated
choices.why: ECE was 0.108.

choices.text: A Brier of 0.212 is an excellent score for a model
choices.why: Lower is better, and a constant did better.

prompt: *On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks* (Guo and others, 2017) studied calibration. What did it find?
hint: Compare the networks of 2017 with older ones.

choices.text: Language models state well-calibrated confidences
choices.why: The paper was about classifiers' computed probabilities, not stated numbers.

choices.text: Larger networks were better calibrated
choices.why: The opposite: modern, deeper networks were more overconfident.

choices.text: Newer deep nets were more overconfident than older ones
choices.why: Right, and a single rescaling, temperature scaling, fixed much of it.

choices.text: Calibration cannot be measured without a person
choices.why: It needs labels, which people gave, and then it is arithmetic.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson give as rules for a stated confidence? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three rules, the same as for any output.

choices.text: Measure it against labels a person gave
choices.why: Yes: reliability table, ECE and Brier.

choices.text: Choose a threshold on one set and report it on another
choices.why: Yes: the set you chose on is a best case.

choices.text: Re-measure when the prompt, the model or the messages change
choices.why: Yes: calibration belongs to all three together.

choices.text: Trust it once the model is large enough
choices.why: Size is not a measurement.

prompt: Put the steps of putting a confidence threshold into production in order.

Choose a threshold on one labelled set
Check that threshold on a second set
Re-measure when the prompt, model or messages change

prompt: A vendor says its model's stated confidence is calibrated, citing an ECE of 0.02 on its own benchmark. What do you do before routing your messages by it?
hint: Whose messages was that measured on?

choices.text: Use 0.98 as the threshold, since the ECE is 0.02
choices.why: ECE is an average gap, not a threshold.

choices.text: Trust it: 0.02 is very small
choices.why: Small on their messages; this lesson's ECE went from 0.064 on dev to 0.270 on the holdout.

choices.text: Ask for the Brier score instead
choices.why: Another number on their benchmark answers the same wrong question.

choices.text: Measure it on your own labelled messages
choices.why: Right: calibration belongs to the model, the prompt and the messages together.
